text: The next day Giovanni called on Professor Pietro Baglioni, an old friend of his father, who received him warmly and spoke with a cheerful ease that softened his learned dignity. <break time="0.8s" /> When Giovanni mentioned Rappaccini, the professor admitted that Rappaccini was as skillful as any doctor in Italy, but warned that he cared infinitely more for science than for mankind. <break time="0.8s" /> His patients interest him only as subjects for some new experiment, said Baglioni, and he would sacrifice human life, his own among the rest, to add a grain of mustard seed to his knowledge. <break time="0.8s" /> Baglioni, whose long rivalry with Rappaccini was well known, added that the daughter was rumored to be so learned that she might already fill a professors chair at the university. <break time="0.8s" /> That evening, from his window, Giovanni watched Beatrice pluck one of the purple flowers, and a drop of moisture from its broken stem fell upon a small lizard creeping at her feet. <break time="0.8s" /> The creature twisted for a moment and then lay motionless in the sunshine, and soon a bright insect, hovering near her face, drooped and fell lifeless at her feet, as if poisoned by her breath. <break time="0.8s" /> Hardly knowing what he did, Giovanni threw down a fresh bouquet he had bought that day, and Beatrice, smiling with a mixture of childish and womanly delight, picked it up. <break time="0.8s" /> As she turned back toward the house, Giovanni fancied that the flowers were already beginning to wither in her grasp, though at such a distance he could hardly be sure of it.
